summary: Singapore lets most nationalities enter visa-free — typically 90 days for US, UK, EU and other Western passports and 30 days for most of Asia, including Chinese citizens under the 2024 mutual exemption, but every traveler must submit the free SG Arrival Card (SGAC) online within 3 days before arrival.

conditionalWaivers.text: Nationals of China, India and the CIS states (Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Moldova, Russia, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Ukraine, Uzbekistan) transiting Singapore by air with a valid US, UK, Canadian, Australian, New Zealand, German, Swiss or Japanese visa can use the 96-hour Visa-Free Transit Facility (transit only, onward ticket required. It is not a tourist entry). The facility is limited to these nationalities.

fee.notes: Processing fee of 30 SGD; authorized visa agents charge an additional service fee. Most applicants must apply through a Singapore-authorized agent or local contact rather than directly.

passportValidity.text: Your passport must be valid for at least 6 months on the date of entry into Singapore.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever vaccination certificate is required if, within 6 days before arrival, you were in or transited through a country with risk of yellow fever transmission.

travelInsurance.text: Travel insurance is not an entry requirement, but medical coverage is recommended — healthcare in Singapore is excellent and expensive for visitors.

onwardTicket.text: You must be able to show a confirmed onward or return ticket; airlines and ICA officers check, and entry can be refused without one.

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published, but you must be able to show sufficient funds for your stay — ICA officers may ask.

declarations.name: SG Arrival Card (SGAC)
declarations.text: All foreign visitors must submit the SG Arrival Card with electronic health declaration online within 3 days before arriving. It is free. Use only the official ICA e-service or the MyICA mobile app.

currencyLimits.text: Cash and bearer instruments totalling more than 20,000 SGD (or equivalent) must be declared on arrival and departure.

notes: There is NO duty-free allowance for cigarettes or tobacco — every stick brought in must be declared and duty paid.
E-cigarettes and vaping products are completely banned — bringing them in is an offense with heavy fines.
Chewing gum (other than therapeutic gum) may not be imported.
Drug offenses carry extremely severe penalties, including the death penalty for trafficking.

payments.text: Cards and contactless payments are accepted almost everywhere, including public transport (foreign contactless bank cards work directly at MRT gates). Cash is only occasionally useful at hawker stalls and small kiosks.

safety.text: Singapore is among the safest countries in the world, with very low crime. Laws are strict and strictly enforced, including for littering, jaywalking and drug offenses.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Singapore Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: Singapore is hot and humid year-round; February–April tends to be slightly drier, while November–January brings the wettest monsoon months.

idp.text: Singapore is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

driving.text: Singapore is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Singapore yet.

tips.text: The SG Arrival Card is free. Third-party websites charging a "processing fee" are unnecessary and often scams. Submit it only at eservices.ica.gov.sg or via the MyICA app, within 3 days of arrival.
Vapes and e-cigarettes are illegal in Singapore — possession or import brings fines that can reach thousands of dollars. Leave them at home.
Singapore has zero duty-free allowance for tobacco. Declare and pay duty on any cigarettes you carry in — undeclared packs found at the checkpoint mean heavy fines.

Fines apply to littering, eating or drinking on the MRT, and importing chewing gum; drug offenses carry the death penalty. Singapore's rules are famous for a reason — follow them and you will find the city extremely easy to visit.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Singapore?
faq.answer: No. US passport holders enter visa-free and are normally granted up to 90 days. The only mandatory step is the free SG Arrival Card, submitted online within 3 days before arrival at eservices.ica.gov.sg.

faq.question: What is the SG Arrival Card and who needs it?
faq.answer: The SG Arrival Card (SGAC) is Singapore's free digital arrival declaration, including a health declaration. Every foreign visitor must submit it online within 3 days before arriving, via eservices.ica.gov.sg or the MyICA app. It is not a visa — visa-required nationals need both a visa and the SGAC.

faq.question: Can Chinese citizens visit Singapore without a visa?
faq.answer: Yes. Since February 9, 2024, China and Singapore mutually waive visas for ordinary passport holders: Chinese citizens can stay in Singapore visa-free for up to 30 days. The SG Arrival Card is still required before arrival.

faq.question: Do Indian citizens need a visa for Singapore?
faq.answer: Yes. Indian passport holders need an entry visa before traveling, with a processing fee of 30 SGD (agents add their own service fee). Applications go through Singapore-authorized visa agents or a Singapore mission, and visas are typically issued as multiple-entry. The SG Arrival Card must also be submitted before arrival.

faq.question: Can I bring cigarettes or a vape into Singapore?
faq.answer: Cigarettes: only if you declare them and pay duty — Singapore grants no duty-free tobacco allowance at all. Vapes and e-cigarettes: no, they are banned outright, and importing or possessing them is an offense with heavy fines.
